sources.headline: Student protesters attack government buildings in Albania
sources.text: Image source, ReutersImage caption, The scene in Tirana, Albania's capital on WednesdayByRachel FlynnThousands of students have taken to the streets in the Albanian capital of Tirana, attacking several government buildings on the second day of violent anti-government protests.The demonstration began outside the ministry of education on Tuesday, as students called for better university conditions and job prospects. Wednesday saw part of the education ministry's building set on fire, while the prime minister's office, finance and interior ministry, and several surrounding businesses were also attacked.Albania's Deputy Prime Minister ​Albana Koçiu has called for "calmness, self-restraint and maturity" and said "Albania does not need to burn to change".Image source, ReutersImage caption, Dozens of protesters wearing gas masks and balaclavas were seen throwing rocks and firecrackers through the education ministry's gatesRiot police have clashed with the protesters, using tear gas and water cannons to disperse them. One demonstrator, Enida Bimi, told Reuters news agency that the protest is not just for the students, but "for all the people of Albania". "The people are very angry at the system. They need to change everything. With this corruption all around, the crime and everything else is happening. And the people now are angry. They need to change the system," Bimi said. Another protester, Arber Leshi, said people are angry at "the most corrupt government our country has ever seen". Education Mirela Kumbaro said that while she respects the right to protest, "civic student protest and violence against public buildings and property are two different things".Image source, ReutersImage caption, Protester Enida Bimi said people "are very angry at the system"Officials have criticised the behaviour of some protesters."Setting fire to an institution is not a peaceful protest. It is an act that endangers peoples lives", said economy minister Delina Ibrahimaj, responding to a video appearing to show protesters throwing rocks at the finance ministry building.Sixteen people were arrested "in connection with violent acts" during Tuesday's protest, Albania's state-run news agency said. Sali Berisha, the leader of the opposition - the Democratic Party of Albania - has praised the protesters. "The streets and squares of Tirana have never seen lions like these students," he said during an evening meeting on Wednesday, Albania's state-run news agency Ata reported.This student-led protest comes after months of anti-government protests, known as the Flamingo Revolution, which is calling for Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign. The protests were sparked by a luxury tourism project linked to Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, which fuelled anger over alleged corruption and a lack of transparency from Rama's government.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Central Tirana on Wednesday evening

sources.headline: Albania’s prime minister vows not to resign over student-led protests
sources.text: Albania’s prime minister has said he will not resign as a protest movement, initially prompted by a proposal to build a Trump family-backed resort in the Balkan state, turned violent with clashes convulsing the capital for a third consecutive day.Speaking on Thursday after calls by students who this week assumed control of the anti-government demonstrations that have rattled Tirana since June, Edi Rama said: “Governments are changed through democratic elections. We had elections last year, not a revolution.”Rama’s comments to Reuters came hours before fresh clashes erupted outside the education ministry, where riot police responded to rock-throwing youths with teargas and water cannon. “My responsibility is to listen, address legitimate concerns and keep Albania moving forward,” he added.The alternative, he argued, would be tantamount “to a betrayal of the Albanians who gave me a strong mandate to complete negotiations on European Union membership … I will not allow violence to derail Albania’s European future.”Rama, who won a historic fourth term last year, has vowed to get what was once the continent’s most isolated Stalinist state into the 27-member bloc by 2030.Edi Rama, pictured earlier this summer, has promised to secure EU membership for his country by 2030. Photograph: Malton Dibra/EPAThe unrest – in contrast to the largely peaceful protests of recent months – marks the veteran leader’s biggest challenge yet.On Thursday, after a night of running street battles between demonstrators and riot police, residents awoke to see the facades of shops smashed and traffic signals destroyed, with government buildings and banks burned and ransacked. An estimated 89 people, including 61 police officers, were injured.The renewed violence has created an atmosphere of unpredictability amid predictions that public patience may finally be running out for the socialist government after 13 years in power.“Young Albanians are tired of all the corruption, tired of all the arrogance. They want to live in a better country and they are not afraid to use violence,” said Afrim Krasniqi, the director of the Albanian Institute for Political Studies in Tirana. “There is no prognosis. Nobody can say what will come next.”But Rama, who emerged from the protest movement himself – becoming the face of state violence when he dared to criticise Albania’s first-post-communist government 30 years ago – also doubled down.“Students are the future. They are the ones who look ahead, who want to go further and faster,” he said as he visited the fire-damaged premises of Tirana’s College of Europe on Thursday. “Today, this is the ruin left by hands that are not, and can never be, the hands of students. These are the hands that try to push Albania down every time Albania tries to rise.”While he was willing to talk with the younger generation about the rising costs of education – a central complaint that has also spurred the unrest – vandalism would not be tolerated, he said.A hooded protester throws a petrol bomb at the College of Europe in Tirana on Wednesday night. Photograph: Hameraldi Agolli/APFor nearly five months, demonstrators have gathered daily outside Rama’s office, prompted by plans for a controversial tourism complex championed by the US president’s son-in-law Jared Kushner. The venture foresees construction along pristine coastline deemed a conservation zone of unique natural beauty, including the uninhabited island of Sazan.Labelled the “flamingo revolution” because of the risk posed by the development to wildlife and delicate ecosystems, the rallies have attracted crowds big and small. They, too, have demanded the prime minister resign.Despite the opposition, Rama has steadfastly refused to back down, defending the project as a “gift” that will boost the economy and provide badly needed jobs by transforming Albania into a high-end tourist destination.Police fired water cannon and teargas at protesters in the capital on Thursday. Photograph: Malton Dibra/EPABut Krasniqi said he believed the protest movement was at an inflection point – even if the demonstrations had also been inspired by similar student unrest sweeping Europe, particularly France.“I think this week we reached a turning point,” he said. “The government had more than four months to talk to people, who every day have been out on the street. It chose to belittle and dismiss them instead. And now students have joined in, and they appear to have the upper hand.”For the first time, Krasniqi said, he had heard young people saying they were prepared to be hurt or go to jail if that was the price “for ensuring democracy”.“Their demands are very different to the [flamingo] protesters. They want better education, better university buildings, a society that offers them hope. They also don’t believe Albania should be for sale.”At €4bn (€3.37bn), the Trump family-backed resort would be the biggest investment the nation has seen.Last week, addressing the controversy triggered by the project, Kushner admitted he and his investment firm, Affinity Partners, were “betting on a country that has never had a project of this scale”.A masked protester prepares to hurl an object. Photograph: Florion Goga/Reuters“There are no guarantees,” he said. “We are taking that risk because we believe in Albania and we believe in Albanians. If successful, the project would represent approximately €4bn of investment and create significant jobs, economic activity and international visibility for Albania.”This week environmentalists, who first led the charge against the development, begged to differ. Months after the protests began, people still felt as exercised about a venture many believed would only benefit the elite, said Aleksandër Trajçe, who heads the country’s leading conservation group, the Protection and Preservation of Natural Environment in Albania.“Anger over the [Kushner] project has prepared the ground for the violence we are seeing, because day after day protesters have been faced with the arrogance of a government that has refused to listen to them, or give an inch.”

sources.headline: Albania’s PM dismisses calls to resign as student protests spread
sources.text: Prime Minister Edi Rama condemns ‘chaos’ as protests continue for a third day in the capital and spread to other cities.Albania’s prime minister has dismissed calls for his resignation as thousands of protesters clash with riot police in the capital for the third day in a row, leaving government buildings damaged.“My responsibility is to listen, address legitimate concerns and keep Albania moving forward,” Prime Minister Edi Rama said in a written statement to the Reuters news agency, following protester demands for him to resign.Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Land sold for Kushner-backed Albania resort suspected of forged deedslist 2 of 3‘Flamingo Revolution’ enters 100th day against Kushner-linked resortlist 3 of 3Protesters, police clash in Albania over Trump-linked projectend of list“The alternative would be a betrayal of the Albanians who gave me a strong mandate ‌to complete negotiations on European Union membership,” Rama added on Thursday.This comes as riot police used water cannons and tear gas against crowds of protesters in the capital, Tirana. Demonstrators have accused officials of corruption and neglecting education, ⁠expressing anger about the sale of parts of Albania’s southern coastline to a luxury resort development backed by United States President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.Tirana’s streets were littered with burnt-out rubbish bins, shattered bus stops and broken traffic lights. In the capital’s central Skanderbeg Square, police hit fleeing protesters with batons as tourists looked on.Thursday’s protests also spread to several smaller cities as students joined university boycotts.Rama, whose government denies corruption, said he would be ready to discuss rising education costs but rejected the calls to resign.“Perhaps some forces, at home and abroad, do not want Albania to succeed as a forerunner for EU membership. But I will not allow violence to derail Albania’s European future,” Rama said in his statement to Reuters.Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama has denied allegations of government corruption [File: Leon Neal/Getty Images]‘Everyone will certainly pay’Rama earlier posted a video on his Facebook page showing him touring the burnt-out remains of an office at a university campus in Tirana.“Until yesterday, this was the office of the College of Europe, the school of a united Europe,” he said in the video, his first public comments since the protests began.“Everyone is responsible before the law, and everyone who has had a hand in this chaos will certainly pay.”The prime minister was due to meet his party’s parliamentary group early on Thursday, when protesters circulated an “ultimatum” demanding his resignation by 1pm (11:00 GMT).But even before the deadline passed, protesters had already begun clashing with police, building makeshift barriers and setting fire to bins.‘Our prime minister is the meaning of the word corruption’A student who gave her name as Kiara told Reuters the cost of living, poor job prospects and alleged corruption were the main issues for protesters.“Our prime minister is the meaning of the word corruption. You can only find work in your field if you know a guy who knows a guy,” she said, her face covered by a mask, like many on the streets on Thursday.Police detain a protester during an anti-government demonstration in central Tirana on Thursday [AFP]The protesters demanded Rama’s resignation, saying no one had listened to their concerns during a summer of largely peaceful protests over the luxury resort development linked to Kushner.Police said 65 people were arrested during Wednesday’s protests, suspected of “attacking police officers, institutions, public and private property”.The Health Ministry said in a statement that hospitals in Tirana treated 89 people on Wednesday, including 61 police officers.Four officers and two protesters remained hospitalised, with a demonstrator and two officers expected to undergo surgery.“Attacking institutions, destroying public property and threatening public safety have nothing to do with the legitimate demands of students,” Rama said.

Student Protests in Albania Turn Violent as Calls Grow for Leader’s Resignation

Opposition to a luxury resort project linked to Jared Kushner has collided with rising discontent over corruption and the cost of living.

Listen · 5:55 min
Share full article
A protester confronting riot police during an anti-government demonstration in central Tirana, Albania, on Thursday.
Credit...
Adnan Beci/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

By Fatjona MejdiniPaul Mozur and Lynsey Chutel

Fatjona Mejdini and Paul Mozur reported from Tirana, Albania.

Oct. 15, 2026, 12:20 p.m. ET
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Add The New York Times on Google 

Thousands of students, setting fires in the streets and barricading roads with wrought ironwork, brought Albania’s capital to a standstill on Thursday, as anger over the high cost of education coalesced into violent protests demanding the prime minister’s resignation.

The police responded with tear gas and water cannons, arresting dozens and charging nearly a hundred people in all. But little seemed to tamp down the growing pressure on Prime Minister Edi Rama of Albania, as public opposition to a luxury resort project linked to President Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner collided with growing discontent over corruption and the rising cost of living.

This week, months of demonstrations over those issues snowballed into violent protests in Tirana, Albania’s capital, where the education costs brought high schoolers, university students and others into the streets.

Image
Flames engulfing a kiosk during clashes between police and demonstrators in Tirana on Thursday.
Credit...
Florion Goga/Reuters

As they marched to the education ministry and the prime minister’s office, some set fire to trash cans and bus shelters, pelted government buildings and banks with rocks and clashed with the police.

“Albanians have been protesting for more than four months, demanding the prime minister’s resignation, but no one has paid attention to their demands,” said Anila Shehu, a third-year engineering student. “For this reason, we will continue to protest by any means and in any way possible until Rama resigns. Enough is enough.”

sources.headline: Albania: Fire at Education Ministry as students protest
sources.text:
Albania's Education Ministry caught fire on Wednesday in a second day of student protests over corruption and education.
The scenes were at least somewhat reminiscent of the protracted student demonstrations in France in recent weeks.
They are probably the most violent outburst of low-level anti-corruption protests against Prime Minister Edi Rama's government and the main opposition led by Sali Barisha that started in May this year.
Many of the demonstrators wore face coveringsImage: Florion Goga/REUTERS
What happened in Tirana's student protests?
Police deployed riot police and used tear gas and water cannons to disperse crowds in the capital Tirana. Thousands of protesters gathered in front of the Education Ministry on Wednesday, many obscuring their faces. Some threw bricks at the building, damaged barriers on the sidewalks and overturned trash cans.
A bank near the Education Ministry also caught fire, according to the Reuters news agency citing a witness.
The demonstration started on Tuesday with a peaceful gathering of several hundred people outside the Education Ministry but quickly escalated and turned violent in places.
Police early on Wednesday reported around 40 detentions and 13 people injured, including six police officers. Unrest continued long after these figures were issued.
Police used tear gas and water cannons on demonstrators in parts of TiranaImage: Florion Goga/REUTERS
Government says demonstrations degenerated into 'orchestrated violence'
Deputy Prime Minster Albana Kociu posted a video of demonstrations on Facebook saying it was "disheartening to see the culture of protest degenerate into orchestrated violence."
She said that the attacks on institutions and police and the "senseless destruction of public property" were "not the language through which the youth should express themselves." Instead, she said they were reminiscent of the "old habits of those who use young people to mask their own political incompetence."
In another post, Kociu called on students who believe in the right to protest to "distance" themselves from "violence and vandalism."
Student organizers say the protests revolve around conditions at universities, higher education costs, financial support and employment prospects after graduation.
More generally, Albania has faced a series of demonstrations this year sometimes referred to as the "Flamingo Revolution." These were at least partly prompted by a controversial construction project on the Adriatic Coast in a protected area where flamingos live.
But these partly environmental protests have also had a more general theme of dissatisfaction with Albania's dominant political forces. PM Edi Rama's Socialists and Sali Barisha's right-wing Democrats have alternated in government for more than 30 years, ever since the post-Cold War democratic transition in the former communist country. Albania: Europe's new billionaire playgroundTo view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
The timing is also conspicuous, with the demonstrations starting amid prominent international coverage of widespread school and student protests in France in recent weeks leading to similarly restless scenes.
Edited by: Wesley Dockery

sources.headline: Albania: Violent protests rock Tirana for third straight day
sources.text:
Demonstrators hurled stones, firecrackers and other objects at riot police, who responded with tear gas and water cannon. Fires broke out in the city centre, engulfing trees and a roadside structure as firefighters worked to contain the flames.
Footage shows protesters racing through smoke-filled streets, tearing down police barriers and throwing tear-gas canisters back at officers. Shops and banks were damaged, some looted, while police reported vandalism targeting ATMs, cameras, vehicles and fencing. Burnt-out vehicles, smashed windows and wrecked offices were left behind across the Albanian capital, where residents and workers began clearing debris as demonstrations continued.
What began three days ago as student protests over the cost and quality of higher education has become a broader challenge to Prime Minister Edi Rama's government. Students demanding better university conditions, financial support and job prospects have joined the Flamingo movement, which opposes a luxury resort project linked to Jared Kushner and is calling for Mr Rama's resignation over corruption allegations.

sources.headline: Albania police use tear gas on protesting students as stir turns violent
sources.text: In Albania, student protests escalated into violent clashes with police in the capital, Tirana.Student demonstrations in Albania turned violent on Tuesday as protesters threw bricks and concrete blocks at the education ministry in the capital, Tirana. Police responded by firing tear gas and deploying water cannons to disperse the crowd.Several demonstrators were detained by police during the nationwide protest, which focused on education-related concerns and broader social grievances.Student organisers said the rally was intended to draw attention to challenges facing university students, including campus conditions, the cost of higher education, financial assistance and employment opportunities after graduation.Some participants also expressed anger over social inequality and the government's policies, calling for fundamental political and social change.“What Albania needs is a revolution, a change, a complete overthrow of the system because it can't go on like this,” protester Luljeta Kola said. She highlighted what she described as widespread social injustice and a significant gap between the rich and the poor.Student activism spreads across EuropeThe protest in Albania comes against the backdrop of growing student activism in several European countries. In France, high school students have held weeks of demonstrations and blocked school premises to demand more teachers and better facilities.The protesters there have raised concerns that deteriorating school buildings and overcrowded classrooms are affecting the quality of education.Albania's deputy PM criticises violent demonstrationsAlbanian Deputy Prime Minister Albana Koçiu condemned the violence in a Facebook post, arguing that attacks on public institutions and law enforcement were not appropriate ways for young people to voice their concerns.“Violence has not been, is not, and will never be a solution,” Koçiu wrote. She also criticised stone-throwing, attacks on state police and the destruction of public property, saying such actions were not an acceptable form of youth expression.

sources.headline: Albanian students protest over education, jobs, clash with police
sources.text: Oct 13 - Student protesters hurled bricks and concrete blocks at Albania's Education Ministry in Tirana on Tuesday and police fired tear gas and water cannons in response, as a nationwide demonstration over education and social issues turned violent.Police officers detained several protesters.Student organisers said the protest was over conditions at universities, higher education costs, financial support and employment prospects after graduation.Some protesters added they wanted to express their frustration with inequality and the government."What Albania needs is a revolution, a change, a complete overthrow of the system because it can't go on like this," protester Luljeta Kola said, adding there was deep social injustice and a gulf between rich and poor in the country.The demonstration comes amid a broader wave of student activism in Europe. In France, high school students have staged weeks of protests and school blockades demanding more teachers and better facilities, arguing that deteriorating school buildings and overcrowded classrooms are undermining education.Albania's Deputy Prime Minister Albana Koçiu wrote on Facebook: "Violence has not been, is not, and will never be a solution. Throwing stones, attacking institutions and the state police, as well as the senseless destruction of public property, are not how youth should express themselves." REUTERS
